medical.title: Putting paternal mental health in the spotlight
medical.summary: The mental health of fathers and partners can be overlooked during the transition to parenthood, yet depression and anxiety are twice as common among expecting and new fathers as global estimates for men. Through her research at the Centre for Health Services Studies (CHSS), Dr. Sharin Baldwin is building evidence to better support fathers' mental health and inform national research on family health and well-being.

medical.title: Balloon technique may help improve circulation to heart and brain during cardiac arrest
medical.summary: A procedure to inflate a balloon in the body's largest artery to temporarily send more blood to the heart and brain may help improve the low chance of survival (1 in 10) for people who experience cardiac arrest outside of the hospital, according to new, independent, preliminary late-breaking science presented Saturday at the American Heart Association's Resuscitation Science Symposium 2026 in Chicago.

medical.title: Wildlife import linked to higher risk of animal-human disease outbreaks
medical.summary: In recent research published in the journal One Health, "Exploring the Impacts of Wildlife Trade on Zoonotic Spillover and Disease Outbreaks: A Multiple-perspective Study," researchers from Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University (XJTLU) have discovered that wildlife imports strongly influence the likelihood of zoonotic emerging infectious disease (EID) outbreaks. This marks the first global measurement of how wildlife trade is linked to outbreaks of animal-borne diseases, across countries and over time.

medical.title: How human movement predicts health measures across multiple body systems
medical.summary: Newton Tech, a developer of AI-powered movement intelligence technology for clinical research, has published a new study it co-authored in Nature Medicine showing that artificial intelligence can reveal extensive health information encoded in subtle patterns of human movement. In 3,328 adults, the model identified significant associations with 1,887 of 3,210 health measures spanning 18 body systems, from blood tests and liver imaging to sleep, mental health and clinical diagnoses.

medical.title: Dark nutrition: What happens when people stop trusting food and nutrition science?
medical.summary: "I'm Pi and this is Leo, and today we're going to eat some raw roadkill." So begins a YouTube video featuring two raw food enthusiasts eating the heart of a run-over raccoon.

medical.title: AI-interpreted echocardiograms comparable to human reports, cardiologists' time cut by about 50%
medical.summary: AI-generated interpretations of echocardiograms were comparable in accuracy to preliminary interpretations prepared by ultrasound technicians (sonographers) and cardiologists. The assistance of AI preliminary interpretations also reduced the time cardiologists spent interpreting each scan by almost half. All of this is according to new, independent, preliminary late-breaking science presented Monday at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago.

medical.title: Slow hands, quiet nights? Tai chi and a matched exercise class nudged sleep about equally in older men after cancer
medical.summary: Sleep disturbances affect up to 60% of people after primary cancer treatment, and they are often waved away as the price of treatment, or of age. For older men in particular, science has had little to offer. Most research on behavioral treatments for insomnia has studied women with breast cancer.

medical.title: Scientists finally discover why we learn to love bitter coffee
medical.summary: Scientists have uncovered a hidden gut-to-brain dopamine pathway that helps explain why bitter coffee and other initially unpleasant flavors can become favorites over time. The discovery reveals how the brain learns to crave certain foods and could eventually lead to new ways of reshaping eating habits and food preferences.

science.title: Autumn Mornings Bring Valley Fog
science.summary: Low clouds trace the branching valleys of the Appalachian Plateau and the Cumberland River, then burn off by afternoon.

science.title: Math anxiety may be stopping students from learning useful AI and data skills
science.summary: Artificial intelligence is increasingly becoming part of everyday life and work. AI can generate information, summarize evidence and perform calculations. However, it does not remove the need for critical thinking and conceptual understanding.

science.title: Light-pulse pairs reveal the femtosecond decay of an inner-shell hole in xenon atoms
science.summary: Researchers at the UVSOR Synchrotron Facility (Institute for Molecular Science, Japan) and partner institutions have observed the decay of a xenon 4d core hole, an inner-shell vacancy, directly in the time domain. They used pairs of phase-coherent extreme ultraviolet pulses from a synchrotron to make the photoelectron wave packets they released interfere. The contrast of the interference fringes decreased over a few femtoseconds as the delay between the pulses increased. A model using literature core-hole lifetimes of about 6 femtoseconds reproduced this rapid decay of the fringe contrast. The study is published in the journal Physical Review A.

science.title: AI-assisted atomic models reveal how protective shells regulate aluminum nanoparticle oxidation
science.summary: Building an accurate model of how atoms interact is a complicated process. Researchers must choose new calculations, test successive models and track the mechanisms behind each interaction. But a newly developed AI agent called MLP Copilot has made this process much easier by bridging computational tools and scientific evidence with human supervision.

science.title: Barium titanate's optical properties emerge more clearly after decades of widely varying measurements
science.summary: A KAIST-led research team has characterized how light propagates through and is absorbed by barium titanate (BTO), a promising material for next-generation optical communication devices. By clarifying optical properties that had been difficult to determine because of the material's complex internal structure, the study provides a foundation for designing these devices.

science.title: Electrical technique concentrates milk without using heat, challenging traditional preservation methods
science.summary: Dehydrating milk to turn it into powder is, today, an energy-intensive process that subjects the product to high temperatures. Powdered milk is widely used by the food industry and allows the product to be stored and transported in a stable condition for long periods of time without the need for refrigeration. While industrial methods are effective, they have high energy costs and can alter heat-sensitive components, such as whey proteins, enzymes or vitamins.

science.title: Fossil CO₂ emissions projected to decrease in 2026 amid clean energy growth and Iran conflict
science.summary: Global carbon emissions from fossil fuels are projected to decrease by 0.4% in 2026—driven by expansion of solar and wind power and the Iran conflict—according to new research by the Global Carbon Project. The 2026 edition (the 21st annual report) is published in the journal Earth System Science Data.

science.title: After 40 years, CERN finds evidence of a one-in-10-billion particle decay
science.summary: CERN scientists have finally found evidence of a particle decay so rare that it happens only once in roughly 10 billion decays, ending a search spanning more than 40 years. The breakthrough could help physicists uncover hidden particles and forces that lie beyond the reach of today's most powerful accelerators.

environment.title: Amazon mapping shows cacao expansion without deforestation in Brazil
environment.summary: While West Africa clears rainforest for chocolate, Brazilian farmers are reviving degraded pastures.

The complaints allegedly tie JBS profits to illegal deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon. The Transnational Legal Coalition filed 14 complaints with prosecutors and financial […]

Europe is an important market for Ghanaian timber, international expectations around its legality were changing, and the VPA offered both market access and support for strengthening national forest governance. After a 16-year journey, last year Ghana became the […]

environment.title: A train was delayed by a solar storm. But something didn't add up.
environment.summary: Scientists have cracked a 178-year-old mystery surrounding a train delayed by a solar storm, revealing that the famous incident happened in 1848 rather than 1841. The discovery rewrites the early history of space weather and highlights a threat that still endangers modern power grids, satellites, and communication systems.

environment.title: A massive asteroid slammed into the North Sea and unleashed a 330-foot tsunami
environment.summary: A decades-long mystery beneath the North Sea has finally been solved. Scientists have confirmed that the Silverpit Crater, buried 700 meters below the seabed, was created when a 160-meter-wide asteroid struck Earth roughly 43 to 46 million years ago. The violent collision blasted a towering curtain of rock and water 1.5 kilometers into the air and triggered a tsunami more than 100 meters high.

environment.title: Scientists discover ghostly, eyeless creature hidden in Chinese cave
environment.summary: Deep inside a high-altitude Chinese cave, scientists discovered a ghostly, eyeless freshwater snail that has evolved to live entirely in darkness, marking the first recorded discovery of its kind in China. Named after a faceless mythical creature, the rare species may already be in danger, with researchers finding only three living adults.

environment.title: Scientists discover a plastic-eating “Pac-Man” enzyme with a surprising secret
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered a remarkable “Pac-Man enzyme” that helps bacteria devour certain types of plastic and may offer new hope in the fight against plastic pollution. Researchers found that several biodegradable plastics completely broke down in soil within about a year, while conventional plastic remained largely unchanged.

environment.title: “Crawzilla” was huge. Then scientists found an even bigger crayfish
environment.summary: A nationwide search for giant crayfish uncovered a record-breaking Tennessee specimen and a surprising mystery about how big these freshwater creatures can grow. Scientists found that North American crayfish seem to hit a biological size limit, possibly because of their muscles or protective shells.

mix_items.title: Putting paternal mental health in the spotlight
mix_items.summary: The mental health of fathers and partners can be overlooked during the transition to parenthood, yet depression and anxiety are twice as common among expecting and new fathers as global estimates for men. Through her research at the Centre for Health Services Studies (CHSS), Dr. Sharin Baldwin is building evidence to better support fathers' mental health and inform national research on family health and well-being.

mix_items.title: Balloon technique may help improve circulation to heart and brain during cardiac arrest
mix_items.summary: A procedure to inflate a balloon in the body's largest artery to temporarily send more blood to the heart and brain may help improve the low chance of survival (1 in 10) for people who experience cardiac arrest outside of the hospital, according to new, independent, preliminary late-breaking science presented Saturday at the American Heart Association's Resuscitation Science Symposium 2026 in Chicago.

mix_items.title: Math anxiety may be stopping students from learning useful AI and data skills
mix_items.summary: Artificial intelligence is increasingly becoming part of everyday life and work. AI can generate information, summarize evidence and perform calculations. However, it does not remove the need for critical thinking and conceptual understanding.

mix_items.title: Wildlife import linked to higher risk of animal-human disease outbreaks
mix_items.summary: In recent research published in the journal One Health, "Exploring the Impacts of Wildlife Trade on Zoonotic Spillover and Disease Outbreaks: A Multiple-perspective Study," researchers from Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University (XJTLU) have discovered that wildlife imports strongly influence the likelihood of zoonotic emerging infectious disease (EID) outbreaks. This marks the first global measurement of how wildlife trade is linked to outbreaks of animal-borne diseases, across countries and over time.

mix_items.title: How human movement predicts health measures across multiple body systems
mix_items.summary: Newton Tech, a developer of AI-powered movement intelligence technology for clinical research, has published a new study it co-authored in Nature Medicine showing that artificial intelligence can reveal extensive health information encoded in subtle patterns of human movement. In 3,328 adults, the model identified significant associations with 1,887 of 3,210 health measures spanning 18 body systems, from blood tests and liver imaging to sleep, mental health and clinical diagnoses.

mix_items.title: Light-pulse pairs reveal the femtosecond decay of an inner-shell hole in xenon atoms
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the UVSOR Synchrotron Facility (Institute for Molecular Science, Japan) and partner institutions have observed the decay of a xenon 4d core hole, an inner-shell vacancy, directly in the time domain. They used pairs of phase-coherent extreme ultraviolet pulses from a synchrotron to make the photoelectron wave packets they released interfere. The contrast of the interference fringes decreased over a few femtoseconds as the delay between the pulses increased. A model using literature core-hole lifetimes of about 6 femtoseconds reproduced this rapid decay of the fringe contrast. The study is published in the journal Physical Review A.

mix_items.title: Dark nutrition: What happens when people stop trusting food and nutrition science?
mix_items.summary: "I'm Pi and this is Leo, and today we're going to eat some raw roadkill." So begins a YouTube video featuring two raw food enthusiasts eating the heart of a run-over raccoon.

mix_items.title: AI-assisted atomic models reveal how protective shells regulate aluminum nanoparticle oxidation
mix_items.summary: Building an accurate model of how atoms interact is a complicated process. Researchers must choose new calculations, test successive models and track the mechanisms behind each interaction. But a newly developed AI agent called MLP Copilot has made this process much easier by bridging computational tools and scientific evidence with human supervision.

mix_items.title: AI-interpreted echocardiograms comparable to human reports, cardiologists' time cut by about 50%
mix_items.summary: AI-generated interpretations of echocardiograms were comparable in accuracy to preliminary interpretations prepared by ultrasound technicians (sonographers) and cardiologists. The assistance of AI preliminary interpretations also reduced the time cardiologists spent interpreting each scan by almost half. All of this is according to new, independent, preliminary late-breaking science presented Monday at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago.

mix_items.title: Barium titanate's optical properties emerge more clearly after decades of widely varying measurements
mix_items.summary: A KAIST-led research team has characterized how light propagates through and is absorbed by barium titanate (BTO), a promising material for next-generation optical communication devices. By clarifying optical properties that had been difficult to determine because of the material's complex internal structure, the study provides a foundation for designing these devices.

mix_items.title: Electrical technique concentrates milk without using heat, challenging traditional preservation methods
mix_items.summary: Dehydrating milk to turn it into powder is, today, an energy-intensive process that subjects the product to high temperatures. Powdered milk is widely used by the food industry and allows the product to be stored and transported in a stable condition for long periods of time without the need for refrigeration. While industrial methods are effective, they have high energy costs and can alter heat-sensitive components, such as whey proteins, enzymes or vitamins.

mix_items.title: Fossil CO₂ emissions projected to decrease in 2026 amid clean energy growth and Iran conflict
mix_items.summary: Global carbon emissions from fossil fuels are projected to decrease by 0.4% in 2026—driven by expansion of solar and wind power and the Iran conflict—according to new research by the Global Carbon Project. The 2026 edition (the 21st annual report) is published in the journal Earth System Science Data.

mix_items.title: Slow hands, quiet nights? Tai chi and a matched exercise class nudged sleep about equally in older men after cancer
mix_items.summary: Sleep disturbances affect up to 60% of people after primary cancer treatment, and they are often waved away as the price of treatment, or of age. For older men in particular, science has had little to offer. Most research on behavioral treatments for insomnia has studied women with breast cancer.

mix_items.title: After 40 years, CERN finds evidence of a one-in-10-billion particle decay
mix_items.summary: CERN scientists have finally found evidence of a particle decay so rare that it happens only once in roughly 10 billion decays, ending a search spanning more than 40 years. The breakthrough could help physicists uncover hidden particles and forces that lie beyond the reach of today's most powerful accelerators.

mix_items.title: Scientists finally discover why we learn to love bitter coffee
mix_items.summary: Scientists have uncovered a hidden gut-to-brain dopamine pathway that helps explain why bitter coffee and other initially unpleasant flavors can become favorites over time. The discovery reveals how the brain learns to crave certain foods and could eventually lead to new ways of reshaping eating habits and food preferences.

mix_items.title: Amazon mapping shows cacao expansion without deforestation in Brazil
mix_items.summary: While West Africa clears rainforest for chocolate, Brazilian farmers are reviving degraded pastures.

mix_items.title: A train was delayed by a solar storm. But something didn't add up.
mix_items.summary: Scientists have cracked a 178-year-old mystery surrounding a train delayed by a solar storm, revealing that the famous incident happened in 1848 rather than 1841. The discovery rewrites the early history of space weather and highlights a threat that still endangers modern power grids, satellites, and communication systems.

mix_items.title: A massive asteroid slammed into the North Sea and unleashed a 330-foot tsunami
mix_items.summary: A decades-long mystery beneath the North Sea has finally been solved. Scientists have confirmed that the Silverpit Crater, buried 700 meters below the seabed, was created when a 160-meter-wide asteroid struck Earth roughly 43 to 46 million years ago. The violent collision blasted a towering curtain of rock and water 1.5 kilometers into the air and triggered a tsunami more than 100 meters high.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover ghostly, eyeless creature hidden in Chinese cave
mix_items.summary: Deep inside a high-altitude Chinese cave, scientists discovered a ghostly, eyeless freshwater snail that has evolved to live entirely in darkness, marking the first recorded discovery of its kind in China. Named after a faceless mythical creature, the rare species may already be in danger, with researchers finding only three living adults.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover a plastic-eating “Pac-Man” enzyme with a surprising secret
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered a remarkable “Pac-Man enzyme” that helps bacteria devour certain types of plastic and may offer new hope in the fight against plastic pollution. Researchers found that several biodegradable plastics completely broke down in soil within about a year, while conventional plastic remained largely unchanged.

mix_items.title: “Crawzilla” was huge. Then scientists found an even bigger crayfish
mix_items.summary: A nationwide search for giant crayfish uncovered a record-breaking Tennessee specimen and a surprising mystery about how big these freshwater creatures can grow. Scientists found that North American crayfish seem to hit a biological size limit, possibly because of their muscles or protective shells.
